teaser: A disgraced sculptor, a floating nun and a window you are not supposed to notice.

lesson.text: In 1646 workmen climbed the front of St. Peter's Basilica and began to take down a bell tower, stone by stone. Its designer was Gian Lorenzo Bernini, for twenty years the most powerful artist in Rome. Cracks had appeared in the facade under the tower's weight. His enemies made sure everyone knew whose fault it was.

Bernini was 47. The pope who had protected him was dead, and the new one, Innocent X, preferred his rivals. Big papal commissions stopped coming. For the first time since his teens, he had time on his hands and a reputation to repair.

Then a private client appeared. Federico Cornaro, a cardinal from a rich Venetian family, wanted a burial chapel in the small Roman church of Santa Maria della Vittoria. He gave Bernini something a pope never had: one small space and complete control over it, from floor to ceiling. The work took about five years.

The chapel is said to have cost around 12,000 scudi, a fortune. That was more than some entire churches cost to build in Rome in those years. The colored marbles alone came from quarries all around the Mediterranean.

The church belonged to an order of nuns and friars founded by Teresa of Ávila, a Spanish nun who had died in 1582 and been declared a saint in 1622. Teresa wrote a frank autobiography. In it she describes a vision: an angel, small and very beautiful, standing beside her with a golden spear tipped with fire.

The angel, she wrote, drove the spear into her heart several times. The pain was so sharp that it made her moan, and so sweet that she never wanted it to stop. She insisted it was a pain of the soul, though the body had its share in it. Bernini's task was to carve that sentence. He stayed very close to her words.

lesson.title: The vision, word by word
lesson.text: Two figures in white marble. Read them the way Teresa tells it: first the angel, then herself.

spots.title: The angel's smile
spots.text: A boy with curly hair looks down at her with a gentle, almost teasing smile. He is in no hurry. His calm makes her loss of control stand out even more.

spots.title: The spear
spots.text: A slender gilded arrow, held lightly between the fingers and aimed at her chest. It has been drawn back. Bernini shows the pause between two blows.

spots.title: Her face
spots.text: Head fallen back, eyelids nearly closed, lips parted. This is the moan Teresa describes. The face is smooth and young, though she was in her forties when the vision came.

spots.title: Finger and thumb
spots.text: With his other hand the angel lifts a fold of her robe at the chest, as delicately as you would lift a page. He is clearing the way to her heart.

lesson.text: Now consider what you did not see: her body. Apart from the face, one hand and one foot, Teresa is nothing but cloth. And the cloth does not hang the way cloth hangs. It crumples, breaks and boils. Bernini uses the robe to show what is going on inside her, the way a storm at sea shows a wind you cannot see.
Bernini turns an invisible experience into something physical. The saint's feelings are carved into her clothes, because her body itself is hidden.

Teresa's reform asked her nuns to live poorly and to give up proper shoes, which is why her order is called the Discalced Carmelites, from a Latin word meaning “without shoes.” The bare foot hanging from the cloud is a badge of who she is.

There is a second trick, and it has to do with weight. Marble is heavy, and this group is larger than life. Yet Teresa wrote that during her visions she sometimes felt lifted off the ground. So Bernini had to make several tons of stone appear to hover in front of a wall, and to be lit by something other than daylight.
Three directions organize the niche: one falling, one drooping, one cutting across.

lines.label: Light from above
lines.text: Gilded rods pour straight down behind the figures. Above them, out of sight, Bernini cut a window. Real daylight slides down the gold, so the fake rays seem to shine.

lines.label: The body lets go
lines.text: From her tilted head down to the limp hand and the dangling foot, everything sinks. Nothing in her resists. She is held up by the cloud alone.

lines.label: The spear's path
lines.text: The arrow points along a slant that ends at her chest. Against all the vertical gold, this one diagonal carries the action.

lesson.text: The hidden window is the heart of the idea. From the church floor you cannot find the source of the light, so it reads as heavenly. The cloud is carved rough and left dull, the skin is polished, the rays are gilded wood. Sculpture, architecture, painting and lighting work as one machine. Later writers gave this kind of total staging a name: a unified work of art.

And the staging has an audience built in. On the side walls of the chapel, outside this photograph, Bernini carved members of the Cornaro family in marble, leaning from what look like theater boxes. Some watch, some talk, some read. They turn the vision into a performance, and you into one more spectator.

spots.title: The limp hand
spots.text: Her left hand hangs open over the rock-like cloud, fingers slack. It is the hand of someone who has fainted, and the most relaxed thing in the whole group.

spots.title: The bare foot
spots.text: One foot slips out from under the robe and dangles in the air, touching nothing. It tells you at once that she is not lying on the ground.

spots.title: A cloud of stone
spots.text: The cloud is chiseled into coarse lumps and left unpolished, so it stays gray and matte next to the gleaming robes. Its supports are tucked out of sight at the back.

spots.title: The robe
spots.text: Deep, sharp folds with no logic of gravity. Light catches the ridges and the hollows go black. Try to find the outline of a knee or a hip: you cannot.

spots.title: The angel's tunic
spots.text: His clothing is different: thin, clinging, rippling like flame in a draft, and it slips off one shoulder. Two fabrics, two natures, one earthly and one not.

spots.title: A wing in shadow
spots.text: The feathers of one wing spread behind the angel's raised arm. They are carved in low detail so they stay in the half dark and do not compete with the faces.

lesson.text: Is it too physical for a church? People have asked since the 1700s. A French traveler, Charles de Brosses, looked at Teresa's face and joked that if this was divine love, he knew it well. In Bernini's time the answer was simpler. Teresa herself used the language of the body to describe the soul, and the Church had approved her text.

Bernini was a man of the theater in the literal sense. He wrote comedies, built the sets and the stage machinery, and acted in them. One of his productions reportedly made the audience believe the river Tiber was flooding into the hall.

The gamble paid off. While the chapel was still in progress, Innocent X saw Bernini's design for a fountain in Piazza Navona and gave in: the outcast was back in favor. Bernini, never modest, is reported to have called the Teresa the most beautiful thing his hand had made. It began with a tower pulled down in public.

quiz.question: What setback came just before this commission?
options: Bernini's bell tower at St. Peter's was torn down
quiz.explanation: The tower was demolished in 1646 after cracks appeared, and the new pope sidelined him.

quiz.question: Where did Bernini find the scene he carved?
options: In a dream of Cardinal Cornaro
quiz.explanation: Teresa described the angel and his fiery golden spear in her own account of her life.

quiz.question: Why do the gilded rays seem to glow?
options: They are lit by candles on the altar
They are made of polished glass
Daylight from a hidden window falls on them
quiz.explanation: Bernini cut a window above the niche that visitors cannot see from the floor.

quiz.question: How does Bernini show what Teresa feels?
options: Through the agitated folds of her robe
Through an inscription on the base
quiz.explanation: Her body is hidden, so the crumpled, restless cloth carries the emotion.

quiz.question: What does the bare foot refer to?
options: Her order, the Discalced or shoeless Carmelites
quiz.explanation: Discalced means without shoes, a mark of Teresa's reformed order.

quiz.question: Who watches the scene from the side walls of the chapel?
options: Carved members of the Cornaro family
quiz.explanation: The patron's family appears in marble, as if seated in theater boxes.

facts.text: The commission came from the pope, Innocent X.
facts.explanation: It came from a private patron, the Venetian cardinal Federico Cornaro.

facts.text: The angel in the sculpture is smiling.
facts.explanation: He looks down at Teresa with a gentle smile while holding the arrow.

facts.text: The cloud under Teresa is polished as brightly as her face.
facts.explanation: It is left rough and matte to contrast with the polished figures.
